title: Can a Prenup Protect You From a Spouse’s Debt?

content.rendered:
When couples think about a prenup and debt in Colorado, they often focus first on protecting their separate property and assets. But a prenuptial agreement can address much more than who gets the house or how investments will be divided in the event of a breakup. Prenups can also address financial responsibilities, including debts.

For couples preparing to marry in Colorado, understanding how debt will be handled during their marriage is a way to provide clarity as they move into their new life together.  That clarity can help avoid confusion and conflict later.

How Can a Prenup Address Debt in Colorado?

Yes. A prenuptial agreement should always address the parties’ financial obligations and how they will be handled during the marriage and in the event of a divorce.  Colorado premarital agreements address the rights and obligations of married persons, including agreements about responsibility for bills and debts.

For example, one person may enter a marriage with significant student loans, credit card debt, or business-related obligations. A prenup will establish an agreement between the spouses about whether those obligations will remain the responsibility of the person who incurred them or how certain debts will be treated during the marriage.

This can be especially important when there is a significant difference between the amount of debt each person brings into the marriage.

What About Debt Incurred During the Marriage?

A prenup will also address how debts incurred during the marriage will be paid during the marriage and how they will be treated if the marriage ends.

For example, a couple may agree that certain debts incurred individually will remain the responsibility of the spouse who incurred them. They may also establish how particular financial obligations will be handled in the event of divorce.

However, it is important to understand the difference between an agreement between spouses and the rights of a third-party creditor. A prenup does not automatically prevent a creditor from pursuing someone who is otherwise legally responsible for a debt.

If both spouses sign for a loan, credit card, or other obligation, for example, the creditor will still have rights under the underlying contract. A prenuptial agreement will determine how the spouses allocate responsibility between themselves, but it won’t change the creditor’s rights.

That distinction is one reason careful drafting matters.

Full Financial Disclosure Is Important

Before signing a prenuptial agreement, both parties should have a clear understanding of each other’s financial circumstances.

Colorado law requires transparency and full financial disclosure of the other party’s property, liabilities, and income.

That means debt should not be something that is hidden or overlooked during the prenup process. If one person has significant student loans, credit card balances, business debt, or other financial obligations, those liabilities should be addressed as part of the overall financial picture.

Having an honest conversation about debt before marriage may not be the most romantic part of wedding planning, but it can be an important one.

Should Both People Have Their Own Attorney?

A prenuptial agreement can have significant legal and financial consequences for both parties. Colorado law addresses access to independent legal representation when determining whether an agreement is enforceable. Each party must have a reasonable opportunity to decide whether to retain a lawyer, locate a lawyer, obtain advice, and consider that advice.

The agreement must also be entered into voluntarily and meet Colorado’s requirements regarding financial disclosure and other matters.

For these reasons, it is important not to treat a prenup as a simple form that can be downloaded and signed. The language should reflect the couple’s actual financial circumstances and goals.

Planning Ahead Is A Great Way to Start a Marriage Right

Debt does not have to become a source of conflict after marriage. Discussing financial responsibilities before marriage gives couples an opportunity to understand their options and make decisions together.

A prenuptial agreement may help clarify how certain debts and financial obligations will be handled between spouses, but its effectiveness depends on the circumstances and the terms of the agreement.

If you are considering a prenup and one or both of you have significant debt, assets, a business, or other financial concerns, getting legal advice early will help you understand your options and make informed decisions before you marry.

Ready to Plan Ahead?

A prenuptial agreement will help you and your future spouse establish clear expectations about property, debt, and other financial matters before marriage. If you are considering a prenup and have questions about how it may apply to your circumstances, an experienced Colorado family law attorney will help you understand your options.
